botanical.summary: Plant a friendly leafy hedge of Bana right beside your baby rice nursery to keep bugs and disease away!
botanical.how: Plant Bana (Vitex negundo) alongside the paddy nursery bed.

biological.summary: Crush spiky Ramban leaves and drop them right where water enters your paddy field!
biological.how: Crush fresh Ramban (Agave americana) leaves and place them at the water channel inlet feeding the paddy field.

botanical.summary: A traditional leafy remedy farmers swear by to keep hungry hispa beetles off rice leaves!
botanical.how: Apply ankharein leaves to control rice hispa, following local farmer practice in Kangra and Hamirpur.

cultural.summary: Store harvested grain in a big spindle-shaped bamboo basket—a cozy, breathable, pest-proof home!
cultural.how: Store harvested paddy and finger millet grain in large spindle-shaped bamboo baskets, locally called 'Perru'.

cultural.summary: The fungus rides on the seed and can live in it for years, so clean seed protects the seedlings.
cultural.how: Soak seed in cold water for 8 hours, then dip it in water held at 53-54 °C for 10-12 minutes. Cool in cold water and dry in shade before sowing.

cultural.summary: Brown spot mainly attacks plants that are short of nutrients or stressed for water.
cultural.how: Use well-rotted compost or green manure, avoid letting the field dry out at critical stages, and use seed from a healthy crop.

cultural.summary: Rice on soils low in silicon is more prone to the disease, and some varieties tolerate it much better.
cultural.how: Ask your KVK about tolerant local varieties, and about silicon-rich amendments if your soil is known to be low in silicon.

cultural.summary: Weeds and old straw carry the fungus between seasons.
cultural.how: Keep bunds free of weeds and remove or deep-bury diseased straw and stubble after harvest.

biological.summary: Friendly bacteria on the seed and roots protect against brown spot; this is TNAU's recommended biocontrol.
biological.how: Treat seed with 10 g Pseudomonas fluorescens powder per kg of seed. For transplanted rice, also dip the seedling roots for 30 minutes in a suspension of the product at the pack dose.

cultural.summary: Dense, over-fed crops hold the humid air this fungus loves.
cultural.how: Keep to the recommended spacing, avoid heavy urea or fresh dung, and split fertiliser into small portions.

cultural.summary: The fungus lives at the waterline and on weeds and floating debris.
cultural.how: Drain the field briefly when lesions appear, remove weeds from bunds and skim floating plant debris out of the water.

cultural.summary: Removing the first affected tillers slows the climb up the plant.
cultural.how: Pull out tillers with greyish-green lesions near the water line and take them away from the field.

botanical.summary: Neem cake cut sheath blight in Indian trials, especially together with beneficial microbes.
botanical.how: Broadcast neem cake at about 250 kg per hectare (roughly 100 kg per acre) and mix it into the puddled soil before transplanting.

biological.summary: Combining Pseudomonas seed treatment with two leaf sprays and neem cake cut disease by about 81% in a Tamil Nadu study.
biological.how: Treat seed with 10 g Pseudomonas fluorescens powder per kg. Then spray a 0.2% solution (2 g per litre of water) on the plants 30 and 45 days after transplanting.
biological.frequency: Seed treatment, then sprays at 30 and 45 days

biological.summary: Neem cake plus Trichoderma harzianum cut sheath blight by up to 57% in basmati rice.
biological.how: Mix Trichoderma harzianum culture into compost at the pack dose and apply it with the neem cake before transplanting.
